My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.
“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”
Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.
What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.
Working with organisations, I sometimes see almost the inverse. Experience has taught us a great deal. We know what has failed before, where the controls are, which stakeholders need to be involved and where the organisational or technical complexity lies. All of that experience is valuable, but it can also quietly shape the limits of what we believe is possible.
I’ve started to wonder how often our view of the future is really a reflection of the constraints we’ve accumulated from the past.
Where did the horizon come from? # I was recently looking at a process where an SLA was measured in tens of days. Within that organisation this was normal. It was planned around, measured and perhaps even considered reasonably efficient.
I’ve seen similar activities elsewhere measured in hours.
That doesn’t mean the organisation with the shorter SLA has got it right, or that its answer can simply be transplanted somewhere else. Regulation, risk, technology and the nature of the problem all matter. Comparing organisations without understanding their context isn’t particularly useful.
But knowing that somebody else operates on a radically different timescale changes the question. Instead of asking whether thirty days could become twenty-five, we can ask:
What would have to be true for this to take two hours?
I think one of the privileges of having worked across different industries, organisations and technologies is being able to borrow horizons in this way. You get to see different versions of normal. Something that appears impossibly ambitious in one organisation may be completely routine somewhere else.
I’ve found that useful because it changes the starting point for a conversation. You’re not necessarily importing somebody else’s solution or setting their performance as an arbitrary benchmark. You’re using their experience as evidence that the boundaries of the problem may be wider than the ones immediately visible to you.
Sometimes the most useful thing you can bring into a transformation isn’t an answer. It’s a different reference point.
Organisations carry their history with them # The next question, though, is how our existing horizon came to be where it is.
Most organisational complexity didn’t appear because somebody deliberately set out to make work difficult. Quite often there is a perfectly sensible story behind it. Something went wrong: a release failed, a customer was affected, money was lost or a regulator raised a concern. Perhaps somebody made a decision without the right information or without involving someone who needed to be involved.
We responded to the problem in front of us. We added a review, an approval, another piece of evidence or an additional control. At that moment it may have been entirely the right thing to do. Then something else happened, and we responded again.
Over time, those responses become part of how the organisation works. The people who experienced the original problem move on. Technology changes. Regulation changes. The nature of the risk may change. But the process often remains.
So perhaps nobody ever actually decided that something should take thirty days. Thirty days may simply be the accumulated consequence of a series of individually reasonable decisions made over many years.
I find that distinction important because it changes how we approach transformation. Rather than immediately asking how we reduce thirty days, perhaps we should first understand how thirty days became normal.
Which parts of that timeline manage risks that still exist? Which compensate for a limitation elsewhere? Which exist because of technology we no longer use? Which are genuinely required by regulation, and which have simply become associated with regulation through years of organisational memory?
The current process tells us how the organisation works. It doesn’t necessarily tell us how the organisation needs to work.
Borrow the horizon, not the operating model # There’s an idea here that I think connects with something I took from Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh’s Blitzscaling.
The book deliberately examines an extreme environment: organisations trying to achieve very rapid scale while operating with significant uncertainty. I’m certainly not suggesting that every organisation should attempt to behave like a Silicon Valley hypergrowth company. In many of the environments I work in, doing so would be entirely inappropriate.
What I find useful is the challenge it creates to assumptions about what sensible or responsible management looks like.
Practices that are entirely rational under one set of constraints can become limiting under another. An organisation optimising for rapid growth makes different choices around speed, efficiency and uncertainty from an established organisation operating critical infrastructure. Neither operating model can simply be transplanted into the other.
But looking at the extreme is useful because it changes the reference point. It helps us distinguish between “We can’t do that” and “We have chosen not to do that under our current constraints.” Those are very different statements.
The first closes the conversation. The second invites us to understand the constraints and the choices we’ve made around them. Some will be entirely justified. Others may turn out to be assumptions that have survived longer than the circumstances that created them.
That’s an important part of what I mean by borrowing horizons. Borrow the horizon, not necessarily the operating model.
Risk and frequency # There is something counterintuitive here that I’ve seen repeatedly in technology. When something feels risky, our natural reaction is often to do it less frequently.
Yet one of the most useful lessons I’ve taken from DevOps is almost the opposite: if we want to become good at something, we normally need to do it more often.
That doesn’t mean repeatedly taking the same risk and hoping for a better result. We make the individual change smaller. We automate the things that can be reliably automated. We improve observability, shorten the feedback loop and make it easier to recover when something goes wrong.
The result is that something which used to be an event gradually becomes routine.
I’ve seen releases that once required significant planning, coordination and a room full of people become something teams do many times a day. The underlying need for control hasn’t disappeared. Instead, we’ve changed how that control is achieved and built capability through repetition.
That idea is useful well beyond software delivery. When we do something rarely, knowledge decays between each occurrence and the activity remains exceptional. When we can safely do it more frequently, we create more opportunities to learn, improve and eventually automate parts of it.
This is one reason I think ambition needs more than a bold target. If somebody tells a team accustomed to thirty days that the new target is two hours, it is quite reasonable for them to be sceptical. Their experience tells them something very different.
Borrowing a horizon tells us that a different outcome may be possible. The work of transformation is understanding what needs to change to make that outcome credible.
Looking at the system differently # This is also why I continue to find techniques such as value stream mapping useful. The value isn’t simply in drawing the current process or finding the box with the largest number written beside it. A different horizon gives us a reason to interrogate the system more deeply.
If something takes twelve days, what actually happens during those twelve days? How much of it is work and how much is waiting? Where is judgement genuinely required? Where are we managing risk? Where are we compensating for another constraint in the system? And, perhaps most importantly, which of those things would we design differently if we were starting today?
That last question is becoming increasingly interesting because the capabilities available to us are changing quickly.
AI is an obvious example. There is understandably a lot of interest in identifying activities where AI can improve productivity, but starting with the existing activity can also constrain our thinking.
We might use an LLM to produce in thirty seconds a document that previously took someone three hours to prepare. That’s useful. But if the document then waits four days for somebody to review it, we should probably be curious about the four days as well.
There is also a danger that we assume AI itself must be the answer to each of those questions. It may not be. Sometimes deterministic automation, a policy engine or an existing tool will provide a more predictable answer. In other cases, once we understand why an activity exists, removing it entirely may create more value than automating it.
The important change is that our available capabilities have moved. AI can work with context and information in ways that were difficult to achieve previously. Automation can remove repeatable activity. Modern platforms can make capabilities available on demand that once took weeks to provision. The assumptions that shaped a process five or ten years ago therefore deserve to be revisited.
So the question isn’t simply “Where can we use AI?” or even “What can we automate?”
It’s whether those new capabilities should change what we believe good could look like in the first place.
Making a different future credible # This is where I think borrowing horizons becomes more than benchmarking.
A benchmark tells us how somebody else performs. A horizon helps us imagine a different version of our own organisation.
We can look across industries, at organisations operating at a different scale, at new technologies or simply at teams that have approached the same problem differently. None of those gives us an answer we can copy without thought. What they give us is evidence that the assumptions embedded in our current system aren’t the only assumptions available.
From there, we can work backwards. What prevents that outcome today? Which constraints are fundamental and which have accumulated? What capabilities are missing? Which risks need to be managed differently? Where could shorter feedback loops allow us to learn rather than trying to design the entire future upfront?
That feels more useful to me than simply telling organisations to be more ambitious. Ambition without an understanding of risk is easy. The more interesting leadership challenge is retaining the ability to imagine something radically different after you’ve learned how complicated the world really is.
Perhaps that’s something I want my daughter to retain too.
As she gets older, she’ll inevitably develop a better understanding of why she can’t do everything tomorrow. That’s a good thing. But I hope that understanding risk doesn’t stop her looking at something new and asking, “When can I do that?”
Organisations could probably afford to ask that question a little more often too. Not because somebody else doing something means we should simply copy them, but because their experience gives us another horizon against which to test our own assumptions.
If that is possible somewhere else, what would have to be true for it to become normal here?

Most AI coding setups still look suspiciously like a faster version of the way we have always developed software. A developer asks for a change, an AI model explores some files, writes some code, perhaps runs a few tests, and returns the result. Add more specialised agents and the flow can become more sophisticated — an architect creates a plan, an explorer inspects the repository, a developer implements the change and a reviewer checks the result — but it is still essentially a pipeline.
The more interesting question is what happens when we stop thinking about AI-assisted development as a sequence of activities and instead treat it as a closed engineering loop. The shift is subtle but important: don’t ask an agent to implement a change; ask the engineering system to reach a desired state and produce evidence that it has done so. That changes the architecture quite considerably.
From pipeline to engineering loop # My current local coding environment already uses a set of specialist roles around OpenCode: Architect, Explorer, Developer, Reviewer and Documenter. At first glance, the natural design looks like this:
flowchart LR A[Intent] --> B[Architect] B --> C[Explorer] C --> D[Developer] D --> E[Reviewer] E --> F[Documenter]There is nothing wrong with this, but it has an obvious limitation: the process has an end. If the reviewer identifies a problem, we usually rely on another prompt or another human action to restart the process. A stronger model is a feedback loop.
flowchart TD A[Intent / Requirement] --> B[Architect] B --> C[Explorer] C --> D[Developer] D --> E[Deterministic Verification] D --> F[Semantic Review] E --> G[Evidence] F --> G G --> H{Desired state evidenced?} H -- No --> I[Reason about gap] I --> C H -- Yes --> J[Document / Curate] J --> K[Engineering Memory] K --> BThe core cycle becomes Intent → change → observe → compare → reason → change. That is not particularly exotic; it is the same feedback principle that underpins DevOps, continuous delivery and most mature engineering systems. What changes is that we make the loop explicit for AI.
Engineering against a desired state # Consider a simple request: “Add authentication.” A conventional agent may interpret that as an implementation task, but a loop-oriented system should first turn it into a desired state.
Capability: Authenticated access Constraints: OAuth/OIDC Microsoft Entra No credentials stored locally Acceptance: Unauthenticated requests are rejected User identity is propagated downstream Role policies are enforced Automated tests demonstrate all three That changes the job of the coding system. The developer is no longer trying to write some plausible authentication code; the system is trying to make the observed software state satisfy these conditions. After implementation, the interesting output might be:
Build PASS Unit tests PASS Integration tests FAIL Security checks PASS Architecture checks PASS That failed integration test is not simply an error message. It is evidence that the desired state has not yet been reached, so the loop continues.
The missing piece: engineering memory # This creates another problem: how does each agent understand the software system? Today most coding agents reconstruct context repeatedly from source files, README files, architecture notes, Git history, search results, the current prompt and whatever still fits in the context window. This works remarkably well, but much of the system model remains implicit, and every agent is effectively rebuilding its own partial understanding of the codebase.
That is where I think a knowledge graph becomes interesting — not simply a graph of code, but an engineering knowledge graph.
Beyond a code graph # A code graph might tell us that AuthController CALLS AuthService. Useful, but relatively low-level. What I want the graph to represent is the chain between business intent and observable engineering evidence.
flowchart TD R[Requirement] C[Capability] S[Service / Component] CODE[Code] ADR[Architecture Decision] T[Test] E[Evidence] R -->|SATISFIED_BY| C C -->|REALISED_BY| S S -->|IMPLEMENTED_BY| CODE S -->|CONSTRAINED_BY| ADR R -->|VERIFIED_BY| T T -->|PRODUCES| EOther relationships can sit alongside these:
Component DEPENDS_ON Component API EXPOSES Capability Change MODIFIES Component Incident CAUSED_BY Component Test VERIFIES Requirement ADR CONSTRAINS Component Now an agent is not simply navigating files; it can reason over a model of the engineering system.
The Architect becomes an owner of desired graph state # This changes the role of the Architect agent quite significantly. Instead of merely producing a plan, the Architect can define the desired graph transformation. Imagine asking: “Add Xero integration.” The system may currently know:
Financial Reporting ├── Bank data ├── Donations └── Budgeting The desired state may be:
Financial Reporting ├── Bank data ├── Donations ├── Budgeting └── Xero Integration ├── OAuth lifecycle ├── Tenant mapping ├── Account mapping ├── Transaction import └── Reconciliation rules The engineering task then becomes:
flowchart LR A[Current Graph] --> B[Desired Graph] B --> C[Delta] C --> D[Implementation] D --> E[Evidence]That is a much stronger abstraction than simply generating an implementation checklist.
Explorer becomes the graph hydrator # The Explorer agent then has another responsibility: keep the graph aligned with reality. Some relationships can be discovered deterministically — imports, function calls, package dependencies, API routes, database schemas, Terraform resources, CI/CD pipelines and tests. Others require inference.
For example:
TrusteeService IMPLEMENTS Trustee Eligibility That second relationship is not necessarily visible directly in an AST or import graph. An LLM may infer it from names, usage, documentation and surrounding code, and that distinction matters. I would therefore attach provenance to graph assertions.
{ "from": "svc:trustee-service", "type": "IMPLEMENTS", "to": "cap:trustee-eligibility", "source": "explorer", "provenance": "src/services/TrusteeService.ts", "confidence": 0.91 } The graph should never pretend that an AI inference and a compiler-derived relationship have the same status.
Different kinds of truth # This leads to an important separation: the LLM is not the source of truth, and neither is the graph. I find it useful to think of the system as having several different forms of memory and evidence.
flowchart LR L[LLM ContextWorking Memory] G[Knowledge GraphEngineering Memory] V[GitHistorical Record] R[Runtime & TestsObserved Reality] L <--> G G <--> V G <--> RLLM context is working memory, the graph is structured engineering memory, Git records what actually changed, and runtime behaviour and tests provide evidence about what is actually true. That means the AI reasons over truth rather than owning truth, and I think this is a critical architectural principle for agentic systems generally.
Making the graph practical locally # The next question is less philosophical: where does the graph actually live? My preferred approach is to avoid making the graph database itself the authoritative store. Instead, I would treat Git as the durable source of truth for the semantic engineering model and use a graph database as a fast materialised projection.
flowchart LR GIT[Git Repository] JSON[Canonical Graph Files] LOAD[Graph Loader / Reconciler] DB[FalkorDB] AGENTS[OpenCode Agents] GIT --> JSON JSON --> LOAD LOAD --> DB DB --> AGENTS AGENTS -->|semantic updates| JSONThat gives two useful properties at once: the graph remains diffable, reviewable, versioned and branch-aware, while agents still get fast graph traversal rather than repeatedly parsing flat files.
I would not use one giant JSON file # A single graph.json looks appealing initially, but it will become difficult to review very quickly. I would instead use JSONL and separate the different kinds of knowledge.
graph/ ├── schema.yaml ├── authored/ │ ├── requirements.jsonl │ ├── capabilities.jsonl │ ├── architecture.jsonl │ └── relationships.jsonl │ ├── inferred/ │ └── semantic-relationships.jsonl │ └── generated/ ├── imports.jsonl ├── routes.jsonl ├── dependencies.jsonl └── tests.jsonl This separation matters because these files represent different kinds of authority.
flowchart TD A[Authored Knowledge] B[Deterministically Generated Knowledge] C[AI-Inferred Knowledge] D[FalkorDB Runtime Graph] A --> D B --> D C --> DAuthored knowledge includes requirements, ADRs and intentional relationships and should generally be committed. Generated knowledge includes relationships that can be deterministically rediscovered from source, so there is less value in permanently duplicating all of that in Git. Inferred knowledge may be worth persisting, but only with provenance and confidence.
Why FalkorDB becomes a projection # This is why I would treat something like FalkorDB as a runtime projection rather than the system of record. At startup:
flowchart TD A[Start local environment] B[Start FalkorDB] C[Load authored graph] D[Analyse repository] E[Generate deterministic relationships] F[Load retained inferred knowledge] G[Reconcile graph] H[OpenCode ready] A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G G --> HThe first version can be simpler still: start FalkorDB, reload the graph and go. For a single local development environment, rebuilding the graph is unlikely to be particularly expensive, and later the process can become incremental.
Put a small abstraction in front of the graph # I also would not expose the database directly to every agent. Instead I would introduce something like:
graphctl init graphctl hydrate graphctl reconcile graphctl query graphctl validate graphctl export That gives the agent system a stable interface. The Architect might ask graphctl query capability authentication, Explorer might record a relationship through graphctl add-edge, and Reviewer might ask for constraints affected by the current HEAD. The important point is that the implementation underneath can evolve; FalkorDB today could become something else later without rewriting every agent prompt or tool integration.
Persistent changes should still flow through Git # There is one rule I would keep fairly strict: agents should not freely mutate the graph database and leave the result there. Persistent semantic knowledge should flow back into version-controlled files.
flowchart LR A[Agent] B[graphctl] C[Canonical JSONL] D[Git Diff] E[FalkorDB Projection] A --> B B --> C C --> D C --> EThat means a code change might produce a Git diff containing all of this together:
src/auth.ts tests/auth.test.ts graph/requirements.jsonl graph/relationships.jsonl The engineering model changes alongside the implementation. That feels important; otherwise we have simply created a second, invisible repository inside a database.
The graph makes debugging narrower # One of the most useful outcomes is that failures become easier to contextualise. Imagine simply being told that Test T92 failed. Without structured context, the coding agent may need to explore a large part of the repository. With a graph it can traverse:
flowchart TD T[Test T92] R[Requirement R127] C[Capability C14] S[Service S7] CH[Recent Change] T -->|VERIFIES| R R -->|SATISFIED_BY| C C -->|IMPLEMENTED_BY| S CH -->|MODIFIED| SThe prompt to the agent can now become: “T92 verifies requirement R127. R127 is implemented primarily by S7 and S9. S7 changed in the latest commit and T92 began failing after that change. Determine whether the implementation or the test is inconsistent with R127.”
That is a far more bounded reasoning problem and much closer to how experienced engineers actually debug.
The agents become responsibilities, not necessarily models # At this point, I would describe the system in terms of six responsibilities rather than six separate models.
Architect — intent: maintains requirements, architecture decisions, constraints and desired graph transformations.
Explorer — understanding: hydrates and validates the graph against the repository.
Developer — action: changes code, infrastructure and configuration.
Verifier — observation: executes deterministic checks.
Reviewer — judgement: evaluates whether the evidence satisfies the intended state and whether architectural constraints have been respected.
Documenter / Curator — memory: updates documentation and maintains long-term engineering context.
Around these sits an orchestrator:
while desired_state != evidenced_state: determine_next_action() execute() collect_evidence() update_graph() evaluate_difference() Obviously, I would never make that an unconstrained loop. It needs cost boundaries, iteration limits, permissions and clear escalation points, but as a conceptual model it captures the behaviour I want.
Start smaller than the architecture diagram suggests # It would be very easy to turn this into a platform project, and that would probably be a mistake. My first implementation would be deliberately narrow: a graph schema, authored nodes and relationships stored as JSONL, FalkorDB running locally, a small graphctl utility, static extraction for modules/imports/tests, agent instructions to query the graph before broad repository exploration, and explicit write-back rules for useful semantic discoveries.
Then prove one loop.
flowchart TD A[Architect creates requirement] B[Requirement enters graph] C[Developer changes source] D[Explorer updates relationships] E[Verifier runs tests] F[Evidence enters graph] G[Reviewer evaluates state] H{Satisfied?} A --> B B --> C C --> D D --> E E --> F F --> G G --> H H -- No --> C H -- Yes --> I[Complete]Only after that would I start thinking about embeddings, GraphRAG, automatic ontology evolution or more elaborate multi-agent orchestration.
The bigger idea # What I find interesting is that this is starting to look very similar to the architecture I keep arriving at when thinking about enterprise AI. In the enterprise context: ontology + context + deterministic systems + AI reasoning + agents + memory. In a software engineering environment: software graph + deterministic tools + AI reasoning + specialist agents + Git history. They are really expressions of the same principle.
AI should not own truth. It should reason over a structured representation of truth, act through controlled mechanisms, observe the result, and continuously reconcile its model with reality.
That may turn out to be more important than simply giving coding agents ever larger models or ever larger context windows. The interesting evolution is not just from coding assistant to coding agent; it is from coding agent to engineering system.

title: From Coding Agents to Loop Engineering: Using Knowledge Graphs to Build Better AI Engineering Systems

content:
Technology rarely fails in isolation. More often, the difficult problems sit in the spaces between technology, organisations, incentives, decisions and people.
This site is where I explore those spaces.
I write about transformation, organisational flow, architecture, platforms, AI and the way we design systems around people. Much of it starts with something I have seen in practice: a bottleneck that should not exist, a control that has become friction, a platform that changes how teams work, or a technology that creates a new organisational possibility.
The recurring question is usually the same: how do we create systems that are safer, faster and easier to change without pretending that the difficult parts are simple?
Current themes # Transformation & Flow # How work moves through organisations, what constrains it, and why local optimisation so often makes the wider system worse. This includes value streams, dependencies, operating models, controls, guardrails and the practical lessons I continue to take from DevOps and the Theory of Constraints.
AI & Agency # I am particularly interested in what happens when AI becomes part of the operating system of an organisation rather than an isolated tool. That leads into questions of context, decision-making, enterprise knowledge graphs, agentic systems, trust, sovereignty and where human judgement genuinely adds value.
Architecture & Platforms # Architecture matters most when it changes what teams are able to do. I write about cloud platforms, developer experience, golden paths, internal platforms, modernisation and the relationship between technical architecture and organisational capability.
Leadership & Operating Models # Technology change is rarely only a technology problem. I am interested in the structures, boundaries, incentives and decision rights that shape behaviour, particularly in large and regulated organisations.
Personal Systems # Some of the writing is more personal: note-taking, knowledge management, ADHD, learning and the systems I use to make sense of a fairly noisy world. These ideas often turn out to connect back into the same questions of flow, constraints and attention.
What is coming # The next group of articles is likely to go deeper into the relationship between flow, dependencies, horizons and guardrails, alongside a parallel thread on enterprise context, knowledge graphs, decisioning and agency.
Those two threads are increasingly converging. If AI systems are going to act with greater autonomy, then the quality of the surrounding context, controls and decision structures becomes more important, not less.
That is the territory I expect to spend quite a lot of time exploring here.
The older posts remain part of the site too. Some are rougher, some reflect where I was at the time, but I would rather keep the history than pretend the thinking appeared fully formed.

title: John, Complected

content:
Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV Read alongside: Scripture Psalm 27 NIV There are many things that can make us afraid. Sometimes we know exactly what we are frightened of; sometimes we simply feel afraid and cannot explain why. Our thoughts can become confused, things that once seemed familiar can feel uncertain, and we may wonder what is happening or what will happen next.
But there is something that has not changed: God is with you. He has not moved away from you, he has not forgotten you, and he has not stopped loving you. Again and again in the Bible, God tells his people, “Do not be afraid.” He does not say this because there is never anything frightening in life, but because we do not face those things alone.
Joshua — God was not finished with him # Joshua knew what it was to wait. He had already spent decades serving alongside Moses, watching God lead Israel and learning to trust him. Then Moses died and Joshua found himself facing a new chapter. He was not being asked simply to look back on everything God had already done; God still had work for him to do.
At precisely the moment when Joshua might have felt the weight of the past and uncertainty about the future, God said:
Scripture Joshua 1:9 NIV Joshua’s courage did not come from pretending that nothing frightening lay ahead. It came from remembering who was with him. The God who had been faithful through the wilderness had not changed, and God was not finished with Joshua yet.
That same God is your God. Because you belong to Jesus, God has made his home with you. The Bible says:
Scripture 1 John 4:4 NIV Fear can feel very big. A troubling thought can feel very big. Something we cannot understand can feel very big. But Jesus is greater. You do not have to win every argument in your mind or understand everything that is happening. You can come back to one simple truth: Jesus is with me. Jesus loves me. I belong to Jesus. I do not need to be afraid.
Read Psalm 27 # Psalm 27 gives us words to use when fear feels close. It begins with a question worth holding onto: “The Lord is my light and my salvation—whom shall I fear?” The psalm does not pretend that there are no enemies, troubles or frightening circumstances. Instead, David keeps returning his attention to God: his light, his salvation and his stronghold.
Read the whole psalm slowly. You do not need to remember every line. Notice the repeated confidence that God is present and trustworthy, and finish with its invitation to wait for the Lord and take heart.
Remember # Your feelings can change, your circumstances can change, and even some of the things you remember may become difficult to hold onto. But God does not change. Like Joshua, you can look back on years in which God has been faithful and still look forward believing that he has not finished with you.
Jesus said:
Scripture John 10:28 NIV You are held by him. Your security does not depend upon how strongly you can hold onto God; he is holding onto you. You are still here, still loved, still held, and God is still at work in your life.
Say this together # I belong to Jesus. God is with me. God has not forgotten me. Greater is he who is in me. God is not finished with me. I do not need to be afraid.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you are with me. When I feel afraid, help me remember that I belong to you. Thank you for the example of Joshua and for the reminder that you were still leading him into new things after many years of walking with you.
Thank you that Jesus is greater than anything that frightens me, that you have not forgotten me, and that nothing can take me out of your hand. Help me to remember your faithfulness, trust you for what is ahead, and know that you are still at work in me. Give me your peace today.
In Jesus’ name, Amen.

content:
Read: Scripture Psalm 46:1–7 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Change can be difficult. Sometimes it is not even the change itself that is hardest, but the uncertainty that comes with it. We might know how yesterday worked, but suddenly we are not quite sure what tomorrow will look like.
That can happen when we start somewhere new, perhaps a new school, class or group. We need to learn where we fit, who people are and how things work. But change can happen in familiar places too. Someone we know might begin behaving differently towards us. A friendship might feel different. Something that once seemed easy can suddenly become confusing, and we can find ourselves wondering what we are supposed to do next.
The Bible never promises us a life where nothing changes. In fact, many of the people we read about in Scripture found themselves facing enormous uncertainty. Abraham left the place he knew without knowing exactly where God was taking him. Joseph’s whole life changed when his brothers sold him into slavery. Ruth left her home and began again in a foreign land. David went from looking after sheep, to living in a palace, to running for his life. The disciples left their old lives to follow Jesus, often without knowing what the next day would bring.
What they discovered — and what we can discover too — is that when everything around us changes, God does not.
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
— Hebrews 13:8
The Psalms often describe God as a rock. A rock is strong and steady. It does not move simply because the wind blows or the weather changes.
“The Lord is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer; my God is my rock, in whom I take refuge.”
— Psalm 18:2
That does not mean we will always immediately understand what is happening. Sometimes we would like God to show us exactly how everything is going to work out. We want a map of the whole journey: Who will my friends be? Will I enjoy this? Why is that person acting differently? What happens next?
But Scripture gives us another picture:
“Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.”
— Psalm 119:105
A lamp carried on a dark path does not normally show you everything several miles ahead. It shows you the ground in front of you. You can see enough to take the next step.
Sometimes that is how God leads us. He does not give us every answer at once. Instead, He asks us to trust Him today: to choose kindness today, to have courage today, to tell the truth today, to forgive today, to ask for help today. Then tomorrow, He gives us light for the next step.
Proverbs gives us a similar encouragement:
“Trust in the Lord with all your heart and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways submit to him, and he will make your paths straight.”
— Proverbs 3:5–6
Notice that it does not say we will always understand the path. It says we can trust God as we walk it.
This is especially important when other people change. We cannot control what somebody else thinks, says or does. We cannot force another person to remain the same. But we can ask God to help us decide how we will respond. We can still be kind without allowing someone to treat us badly. We can still forgive while asking a parent, teacher or trusted adult for help. We can be patient when someone is having a difficult time, while remembering that their choices do not have to determine ours.
And when we feel unsettled, God invites us to bring that uncertainty to Him.
“God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear…”
— Psalm 46:1–2
Things around us will change many times during our lives. Schools change. Friendships change. Families grow. Plans change. We grow and change too. Some changes will be exciting and others will be difficult.
But underneath all of those things is something that does not move.
God is still God. He is still good. He is still with us. His Word is still a light for our path, and He is still our rock.
So when we cannot see the whole road ahead, perhaps we do not need to.
We can ask a simpler question:
“God, what is the next right step you are asking me to take?”
And then, holding onto Him, we take it.
Talk about it # Is there anything changing at the moment that feels exciting, difficult or uncertain? When something changes, what are you most likely to worry about? Why do you think the Bible describes God as a rock? What might it mean for God’s Word to be a lamp rather than a floodlight showing us everything ahead? Is there one “next right step” you think God might be asking you to take this week? Things to remember # Psalm 46 describes a world where even the earth and mountains seem to move, yet God remains a safe place in the middle of it all. Psalm 119 gives us another picture: God’s word is a lamp for our feet. We do not need to see the whole journey before we can trust Him with the next step.
Important message # When everything around us changes, God does not. We can trust Him for the next step even when we cannot see the whole road ahead.
Prayer # Father, thank you that you do not change even when the world around us does. When we are excited about something new, help us to enjoy it with you. When we feel unsure or frightened, remind us that you are our rock and our safe place.
Help us not to worry because we cannot see the whole road ahead. Give us enough light for the next step. Give us wisdom when friendships or circumstances change, courage when things feel unfamiliar, and kindness in the way we respond to other people.
Help us to trust you with all our hearts and to remember that wherever we go, you go with us.
Amen.

For younger ones # Read together Psalm 119:105 NIrV Sometimes things change and we do not like it very much.
You might move to a new class. Someone might start playing with different friends. A place that used to feel easy might suddenly feel strange. When that happens, it can make your tummy feel funny or make you wonder, “What do I do now?”
The Bible tells us something very important: God does not change.
He is like a big, strong rock that does not move when everything around it feels wobbly.
The Bible also tells us that God’s word is like a lamp for our feet. Imagine walking outside when it is very dark and you have a little torch. You might not be able to see all the way to the end of the road, but you can see enough to take the next step.
That is sometimes how God helps us. We might not know everything that is going to happen tomorrow, but we can ask Him to help us with today.

What is one small, brave step you could take?
Maybe the next step is to be kind. Maybe it is to say hello to someone new. Maybe it is to tell Mum, Dad or a teacher that something is worrying you.
Things to remember Imagine holding a little torch in the dark. You do not need it to light up the whole road. You just need enough light to see where to put your foot next.
God can help us like that. We can trust Him one step at a time.
Important message God is with me, so I do not have to work everything out on my own. Let’s pray Jesus, thank you that you are always with me.
When things change and I feel unsure, help me remember that you are strong and steady like a rock. Please show me the next step to take, and help me to be brave and kind.
Amen.

Read: Scripture Psalm 46:1–7 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Change can be difficult. Sometimes it is not even the change itself that is hardest, but the uncertainty that comes with it. We might know how yesterday worked, but suddenly we are not quite sure what tomorrow will look like.
That can happen when we start somewhere new, perhaps a new school, class or group. We need to learn where we fit, who people are and how things work. But change can happen in familiar places too. Someone we know might begin behaving differently towards us. A friendship might feel different. Something that once seemed easy can suddenly become confusing, and we can find ourselves wondering what we are supposed to do next.
title: When Things Change

I have been doing a lot of experimentation with local models recently, as have many of my colleagues. There is also a growing anticipation around the next generation of developer workstations and AI-focused boxes: machines capable of running increasingly useful models without sending every request to a SaaS platform.
It is easy to see this as another technology choice: local versus cloud, open model versus proprietary model, workstation versus API. I think the more interesting question for enterprises is economic.
For years, we have invested in developer productivity up front. Powerful laptops and desktops, good monitors, fast build environments and development infrastructure are accepted as part of the cost of enabling people to do their jobs. We do not ask an engineer to demonstrate the business value of every compile before allowing them to run it.
AI has pushed us towards a rather different model.
Every prompt has a cost. Every experiment consumes tokens. At small scale that is relatively easy to ignore, but across a large organisation the uncertainty quickly becomes uncomfortable. If we expect thousands of technical people to use these capabilities continuously, a variable pay-per-use model creates a very different fiscal problem.
The understandable response is governance. Quotas appear. Access is restricted. Teams are asked to justify use cases before experimenting with them. Someone wants to understand the likely return before approving the spend.
All of those things can look fiscally responsible. They can also create exactly the wrong behaviour.
The marginal cost of curiosity # There is an interesting alternative emerging.
What if we treated some AI capability in the same way we treat the developer workstation?
A deliberately higher capital investment — perhaps several thousand pounds more for a developer machine capable of running useful models locally — can look expensive when compared with buying a cheaper laptop. But that is not necessarily the right comparison.
The comparison is between the capital cost of providing reasoning capacity and the ongoing cost of purchasing that capacity by the token.
If our starting assumption is that AI becomes part of the normal technical toolkit, rather than an occasional specialist service, then pre-allocating some of that capacity starts to make sense.
It changes the economics of experimentation too.
Once the machine has been bought, the marginal financial cost of asking another question, trying another approach, generating another test or exploring another idea becomes close to zero. The investment has already been made.
That matters because experimentation is inherently uncertain. If we already knew which experiments would create value, they would not really be experiments.
A funding model that requires teams to demonstrate the value of every possible use before consuming the capability risks suppressing the exploration required to discover that value in the first place.
For the CFO, there is another useful characteristic: predictability.
A known capital allocation to developer capability is much easier to plan than an uncertain curve of token consumption that may accelerate rapidly as adoption grows. This does not make local compute free, of course. Hardware, electricity, support, model management and refresh cycles all have costs. But they are costs we already know how to reason about.
The aim is not simply to make AI cheaper. It is to reduce the cost — and the organisational friction — of curiosity.
The security argument follows the economics # Cost is only one part of this.
A significant amount of enterprise AI governance currently focuses on questions such as model choice, data egress, security boundaries and sovereignty. Those concerns are becoming more important, particularly for organisations operating across regulated industries and multiple jurisdictions.
Enterprise-controlled models change some of that conversation.
If a useful class of experimentation can happen on infrastructure the organisation controls, then we know much more clearly where the data is being processed, what can leave the environment and which models are available. The reasoning capability sits inside a boundary we already understand rather than requiring every exploratory use case to cross into an external sandbox or SaaS service.
That does not remove the need for governance. Models still need to be selected, patched, evaluated and controlled. Sensitive information still needs appropriate handling. Local execution is not automatically safe execution.
But it can make the security and sovereignty model substantially easier to reason about.
More importantly, it can create confidence for teams working with problems they would otherwise be reluctant to explore with an external service.
I increasingly think AI workbench is a more useful mental model than AI sandbox.
A sandbox sounds temporary: somewhere we are allowed to play before doing the real work elsewhere. A workbench is part of the normal environment. It is equipped, controlled and expected to be used continuously.
Not everything belongs locally # None of this suggests that every workload should run on a local or enterprise-controlled model.
The frontier SaaS models remain extraordinarily useful. For some problems the additional reasoning capability will easily justify the cost. Other workloads need scale or capabilities that make centralised services the obvious choice.
The architecture therefore becomes a portfolio rather than a binary decision.
Some reasoning capacity can be provisioned as a predictable enterprise capability. Some can be consumed on demand. Some workloads may never be permitted to leave a particular boundary. Others may deliberately use premium external models because the potential value of the question dwarfs the cost of answering it.
That leads to another problem I find particularly interesting: routing.
Most model routers look at the question being asked and try to infer how capable a model is required to answer it. But the complexity of a question is not the same as its value.
A technically simple question might influence a decision worth millions. A complicated piece of analysis might be little more than experimentation.
How do we know the difference before the question has been answered?
I suspect this becomes less of a reasoning problem and more of a context and memory problem. If the system understands who is asking, what they are working on, which business capability or decision the work supports, the sensitivity of the information involved and the consequences of getting it wrong, then model selection can become an economic and governance decision rather than simply a technical one.
That connects directly to the wider challenge of enterprise context. The more agency we give these systems, the more important the surrounding knowledge, decision structures and guardrails become.
Capacity, not tokens # There is a temptation to treat AI consumption as something entirely new. In some respects it is. But enterprises have dealt with variations of this problem before.
We invest in capacity where we expect sustained use. We consume services where elasticity or specialist capability creates more value. And we build governance around the boundary between the two.
The interesting shift may therefore be less about choosing between local models and SaaS models and more about deciding which reasoning capacity should become part of the standard enterprise environment.
If we believe AI is going to become an everyday part of technical work, then perhaps asking every experiment to justify its token bill is the wrong fiscal model.
The goal should be to create an environment where experimentation is affordable, secure and sovereign enough to happen routinely — while still giving people access to more capable services when the value of the work justifies them.
That feels less like buying AI and more like designing an organisation in which curiosity has somewhere safe to happen.

Over the last few weeks I’ve been writing more.
That has created a slightly unexpected problem.
Writing the article itself was never really the whole problem. I needed somewhere for ideas to start, somewhere they could develop, somewhere finished thinking could live, and a sensible way of sharing it.
For a while those things were all getting mixed together.
I had notes in Obsidian. Drafts developed through conversations. Articles on LinkedIn. Older posts elsewhere. Ideas that were clearly related to one another but were effectively trapped inside individual documents.
What I realised was that I didn’t really need a blogging platform.
I needed a publishing system.
That distinction feels familiar. When I wrote recently about the personal system I use to manage notes, tasks and ADHD, the useful part was never really the choice of tools. It was understanding the problem I was trying to solve, noticing where the friction actually was, and then giving the different parts of the system clear jobs.
I’ve ended up doing much the same thing with writing.
Separating thinking from publishing # Obsidian has become increasingly important to how I work.
It is where incomplete thoughts are allowed to remain incomplete.
An article might start with a sentence, an observation from a client conversation, a diagram, or something that has irritated me enough that I want to understand why.
As I develop it, I want to keep the bits that don’t eventually make the article too: alternative arguments, examples, questions, links to other ideas and things that probably deserve their own article later.
That makes Obsidian a very good knowledge base.
It doesn’t necessarily make it the thing I want to publish.
That distinction turned out to be important.
My working notes should optimise for thinking.
The published version should optimise for reading.
Trying to make one file perfectly fulfil both purposes creates some odd compromises.
A deliberate path from thought to publication # Once I separated those concerns, the publishing flow became much simpler.
flowchart LR A[ObsidianThinking, research and drafts] B[GitHubPublic content source] C[HugoBuilds the site] D[GitHub PagesPublishes the site] E[LinkedInDistribution and conversation] A -->|article is ready| B B --> C C --> D D -->|selected ideas travel to| EThe point isn’t sophistication. It is creating a clear path from a working thought to a published article without making the mechanics heavier than the writing itself.
Git felt like a natural boundary # Once I started thinking about the published article as a separate artefact, GitHub began to make much more sense.
I’ve spent enough of my career around software engineering that source control feels like a fairly natural way of managing something that evolves.
An article has a history.
It changes.
Sometimes I make a small correction. Sometimes an argument develops substantially. Sometimes several related pieces start emerging from the same original thought.
Git gives me a simple record of that without needing to invent another content-management process.
More importantly, committing something creates a useful boundary.
There is a difference between an idea I am still developing in Obsidian and something I am prepared to put into a public repository as part of my published body of work.
That little bit of friction is actually useful.
Why Hugo? # I looked again at conventional blogging platforms, but most of them solve a slightly different problem.
They are very good at providing an interface for creating web content.
I already have an interface for creating content.
It is Obsidian, Markdown and increasingly the tools around my own knowledge base.
What I wanted from the website was therefore relatively modest.
Take Markdown.
Turn it into a fast, simple site.
Give the content enough structure that I can connect things over time.
Stay out of the way.
Hugo fits that model extremely well.
An article is essentially a Markdown file with some metadata around it: title, date, description, categories and some information about how it connects to the rest of the site.
The website itself can then be rebuilt from those files whenever something changes.
There isn’t really a database of articles sitting behind it. The repository is the content.
I like that.
GitHub Pages closes the loop # The final technical piece is GitHub Pages.
The deployment is automated through GitHub Actions. I commit the article, Hugo builds the site, and GitHub Pages publishes the result.
There are obviously many technically more sophisticated architectures I could build.
That isn’t really the point.
The goal is to make publishing cheap enough, cognitively as much as financially, that the tooling doesn’t become another reason not to write.
This is also an interesting evolution of something I was already doing several years ago. I wrote about automating Hugo deployment with GitHub Actions in 2022. The mechanics have changed since then, but the instinct is the same: automate the repetitive part and preserve attention for the part that needs thought.
Giving each platform one job # The more important shift was deciding that each platform had a different job.
flowchart LR A[Obsidian] -->|optimises for| A1[Thinking] B[Hugo site] -->|optimises for| B1[Reading] C[LinkedIn] -->|optimises for| C1[Conversation]That sounds almost trivial written down, but it removed quite a lot of ambiguity.
Obsidian is where the idea is developed and connected to other thinking.
The Hugo site is the durable public version.
LinkedIn is useful for reach, discussion and putting an idea in front of people I already know or who are working on similar problems.
LinkedIn therefore isn’t where I want my writing to live.
It is where I want some of it to travel.
That feels healthier than treating every platform as another place that must contain another identical copy.
A small content operating model # This is probably why the setup feels familiar to me.
I’ve spent a lot of my career thinking about flow, architecture and operating models.
One of the recurring mistakes in all three is allowing the tools or organisational boundaries to define the process.
We buy a system and then gradually reshape the work around what the system expects.
I’m trying to do the opposite here.
Each component has a fairly explicit responsibility.
Obsidian optimises for thinking and connections.
Git provides history and a deliberate publication boundary.
Hugo turns structured content into the public site.
GitHub Pages handles delivery.
LinkedIn provides distribution and conversation.
None of those tools needs to own the entire process.
It is essentially a very small content operating model built around separation of concerns.
Building a body of thinking # There is another reason I’ve wanted to do this.
I don’t particularly want to build a collection of posts.
I want to build a connected body of thinking.
Some of the ideas I’m writing about now have existed in different forms throughout my career. Others are developing very quickly as AI changes what is possible in software, organisations and decision-making.
Those relationships matter.
graph TD Flow[Flow] Dependencies[Dependencies] Horizons[Horizons] Guardrails[Guardrails] Context[Enterprise context] KG[Knowledge graphs] Decisioning[Decision-making] Agency[Agency] VSM[Value streams] OperatingModels[Operating models] OperatingModels --> Flow Flow --> Dependencies Dependencies --> Horizons Horizons --> Guardrails Flow --> VSM VSM --> Decisioning Context --> KG KG --> Decisioning Decisioning --> Agency Context --> OperatingModelsA reader arriving because of something I’ve written about AI should eventually be able to follow the connections into enterprise context, decision-making, knowledge graphs and agency.
Someone reading about transformation might move through flow, dependencies, constraints, horizons and guardrails.
And my own working notes can contain far richer connections than I would ever expose directly on the website.
The public article becomes one expression of a much larger knowledge graph.
That is the direction I find particularly interesting.
The system will probably keep changing # The system I use today almost certainly isn’t the one I’ll be using in a year’s time.
That was one of the lessons from building my personal operating system too.
The objective isn’t to discover the perfect toolchain.
It is to notice the friction, understand what is causing it, and adjust the system.
Right now GitHub, Hugo and GitHub Pages give me something quite simple: ownership of the content, a durable public home, version history, an automated publishing path and enough structure to begin connecting ideas properly.
Obsidian gives me somewhere for those ideas to remain messy before they become articles.
And LinkedIn gives me somewhere to have the conversation afterwards.
The technology is useful.
But the more important change has been deciding that thinking, publishing and distribution are different activities.
Once I separated those, the technology choices became surprisingly straightforward.

Read: Scripture Joshua 1:1–9 NIV Tap or hover over the reference to read the full passage without leaving the page.
Joshua was facing something enormous. Moses had died, and after years of watching Moses lead Israel, Joshua was now responsible for leading the people into the land God had promised them. Thousands of people were looking to him, there were enemies ahead, and Joshua couldn’t possibly know exactly what was going to happen.
Into that uncertainty, God repeatedly tells him: “Be strong and courageous.”
What does being strong mean? # When you hear the word strong, what do you picture? Someone with enormous muscles? Someone who wins fights? Someone who isn’t frightened of anything? Someone who never cries?
What does being strong mean to you? Who do you know that you would describe as strong, and what makes them strong?
It’s easy to imagine that courage means not being scared. But if Joshua had nothing to fear, God wouldn’t need to keep telling him to be courageous. Joshua had plenty of reasons to be frightened. Courage mattered precisely because what he was being asked to do was difficult. Being courageous isn’t the same as having no fear. Sometimes courage means being afraid and choosing to do what is right anyway.
Where does Joshua’s courage come from? # God doesn’t simply tell Joshua to try harder to be brave. He gives him a reason to be courageous: “As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you.” Then, at the end of the passage, God says it again: “For the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”
Joshua’s confidence wasn’t supposed to come from believing that he was strong enough to handle everything. His courage came from knowing who was with him.
Right in the middle of these instructions, though, God also tells Joshua something else: “Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night.” Joshua is told to keep returning to God’s word: to read it, talk about it, think about it and, importantly, do what it says. God’s word wasn’t supposed to be something Joshua occasionally consulted. It was meant to shape how he thought and how he lived.
There’s an important connection here. God tells Joshua to be courageous, reminds him of His presence, and tells him to keep His word continually before him. Joshua would face situations where what he could see gave him plenty of reasons to be afraid. God’s word reminded him of something greater than what he could see.
What about us? # Most of us aren’t preparing to lead a nation into the Promised Land, but we all face things that require courage. It might be something happening at school, a difficult friendship, trying something when you’re worried you’ll fail, standing up for someone, admitting you’ve done something wrong, or simply doing the right thing when everyone around you is doing something different.
So think of something happening in your life right now where you need courage. What would being “strong and courageous” actually look like in that situation? What are you frightened might happen? And what difference does it make to know that God is with you in it?
Perhaps that’s the most important thing to remember from Joshua’s story. Biblical courage isn’t pretending we’re not frightened, and strength isn’t convincing ourselves that we can handle everything alone.
We can be strong and courageous because God is with us.
And one of the ways we learn to trust Him, particularly when what we see around us gives us reasons to worry, is by continuing to come back to His word.
Prayer # Lord, thank you that you don’t ask us to face life on our own, and that you were with Joshua when he faced something far bigger than he could handle himself.
Help us to be strong and courageous, not because we think we can manage everything ourselves, but because we trust you. Give us a love for your word. Help us not simply to read it, but to think about it, talk about it and allow it to change the way we live.
Help us as a family to encourage one another, be honest with one another, and grow closer to you together.
Amen.

For younger ones # Read together Joshua 1:1–9 NIrV Joshua had a really big job to do, and he might have been scared. But God told him: “Be strong and courageous.”
That didn’t mean Joshua had to be the strongest person or that he was never allowed to feel frightened. God told Joshua why he could be brave: God was going to be with him.
Questions to ask Think about something that sometimes makes you feel scared. Maybe it’s going somewhere new, being in the dark, talking to someone you don’t know, trying something difficult, or doing the right thing when someone else doesn’t want you to.
Can you think of something that you have to be brave to do?
Now imagine doing that thing while holding the hand of someone you really trust. Does it feel a little different when you know you’re not doing it alone? That’s what God wanted Joshua to remember. Joshua had a big job to do, but he didn’t have to do it by himself. And neither do we.
Things to remember Put your hand up and make a big muscle. That’s one kind of strong!
Now put your hand on your heart. There’s another kind of strength: choosing to do what is right even when you’re frightened.
Important message Being brave doesn’t mean I’m never scared. I can be brave because God is with me. Let’s pray God, thank you that you are with me when I’m happy and when I’m scared. Please help me to be brave when something is difficult and help me to remember that I don’t have to face things on my own.
Help me to listen to you and learn more about you.
Amen.

I’ve been building a wall of shelves in my office.
Like most DIY jobs, it started with a fairly simple picture in my head and rapidly became a network of dependencies. I couldn’t cut a shelf accurately until the uprights were fixed. I couldn’t fix the next section until I knew how the previous one actually sat against a wall that was considerably less straight than it looked. Some pieces could be measured once and reproduced. Others genuinely had to wait until something else was complete.
Somewhere between measuring another piece of timber and walking back to the saw, I realised there was a familiar organisational problem hiding in it.
We talk a lot in business about managing dependencies. Managing them matters. But I’m increasingly convinced it is the wrong starting point.
A dependency isn’t simply something to put on a RAID log, represent with a line on a programme plan, or discuss at the next coordination meeting. It is part of the design of the system.
And this becomes particularly visible as organisations move towards a product operating model — a journey many of my clients are currently on. Persistent teams with clearer ownership are very good at exposing where the real boundaries are. Once a team genuinely owns an outcome rather than a temporary slice of a programme, the repeated journeys outside that team become much easier to see:
The same security review every release The same infrastructure request The same architecture decision The same data dependency The same team waiting for another team before it can move Those dependencies were often there before. A product model simply makes them harder to hide inside a programme plan.
And broadly, I think there are only three ways to deal with them.
1. Bring it close # The first option is proximity.
If one team is constantly dependent on a particular skill, capability or decision, bring that capability into the team. Embed the security engineer. Put an architect into the product team. Bring the data expertise closer. Create the multidisciplinary team rather than making people repeatedly cross organisational boundaries to get work done.
In the office, this was the equivalent of moving the tools to where I was working. If every adjustment meant walking somewhere else, setting something up, making a cut and returning to see whether it fitted, the transaction cost rapidly became greater than the work itself.
The same happens inside organisations. Sometimes we call this collaboration, but structurally what we have actually done is shortened the dependency. This is often the right answer when the work is ambiguous, highly interactive or changing quickly. It also fits naturally with product thinking: give the team more of the capabilities it needs to own the outcome rather than just its part of the process.
The downside is obvious: you cannot embed every specialist everywhere. Which leads to the second option.
2. Productise it # If bringing the dependency into the team doesn’t scale, turn the capability into a product.
Define the interface. Make the request predictable. Create a service level. Better still, make it self-service.
This is the journey from:
“Speak to Dave in the infrastructure team.”
To:
“Raise this form and somebody will provision it.”
And eventually:
“Choose what you need from the catalogue and it will be provisioned automatically.”
That is much more than automation. It is changing the nature of the relationship.
The dependency moves from white glove to autonomous.
Back at the shelves, once I had worked out a dimension that repeated, I stopped treating every piece as a new problem. I could use the same measurement, the same setup and the same process. The thinking had been turned into a repeatable interface.
This is one of the reasons good platform engineering fits so naturally into a product operating model. A platform team should not simply be a central team that other product teams queue up to talk to. At its best, it takes a recurring organisational dependency and turns it into a product that can be consumed with as little coordination as possible.
The dependency still exists.
The conversation does not have to.
3. Synchronise it # And then there is the difficult one.
Sometimes the dependency cannot sensibly be embedded. It cannot be abstracted behind an interface. The two pieces of work genuinely have to meet. In that case, you have to synchronise.
Plans need to align. Priorities need to align. Capacity needs to be available at roughly the same time. Decisions made by one group need to arrive before another group reaches the point where they are required.
This sounds straightforward on a programme plan. It is anything but. Synchronisation requires two independently operating systems to remain aligned over time, and the moment priorities change in one of them, the dependency starts to drift.
This gets particularly interesting in a product organisation. If two persistent product teams need to constantly coordinate their roadmaps in order to deliver value, then the dependency itself deserves attention.
Perhaps:
The team boundary is wrong A shared capability should be productised There really is a genuine business dependency that needs synchronisation But the answer should not automatically be another cross-team meeting.
This is why I think synchronisation should often be the last choice, rather than the default one. Organisations frequently respond to dependencies by adding coordination: more planning, more governance, more meetings, more programme management. Sometimes that is necessary, but sometimes we are applying coordination to a dependency that should have been redesigned.
Product models expose the joins # One of the useful things about moving towards a product operating model is that it exposes the joins in the organisation.
A project structure can sometimes mask them. A programme manager can chase an action. A delivery plan can contain an assumption. A milestone can move. A dependency can remain visible as a line on a slide without anyone questioning why it exists in the first place.
Persistent product teams make that harder. If the same dependency appears sprint after sprint, quarter after quarter, it starts to tell you something — not just about delivery, but about the operating model.
So when I see a team waiting on another team, I’m trying to ask a different set of questions:
Can we bring the capability closer? Can we productise the interaction? Or do these teams genuinely need to synchronise? Those choices have very different implications.
Bring it close when the interaction is rich and frequent. Productise it when the interaction can be made predictable and repeatable. Synchronise when the work genuinely has to converge.
And perhaps most importantly, don’t confuse synchronisation with dependency management in general. Because if your organisation needs a meeting every week to keep two teams aligned, that might be good coordination. But it might also be telling you something about the way the system has been designed.
Dependencies are inevitable.
A good product operating model helps you see them.
What you do with them is a design choice.

I’ve been building a wall of shelves in my office.
Like most DIY jobs, it started with a fairly simple picture in my head and rapidly became a network of dependencies. I couldn’t cut a shelf accurately until the uprights were fixed. I couldn’t fix the next section until I knew how the previous one actually sat against a wall that was considerably less straight than it looked. Some pieces could be measured once and reproduced. Others genuinely had to wait until something else was complete.
title: Dependencies are a design choice
